https://www.politico.eu/article/ceuta-cr.text: Twenty-two EU leaders — including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni — on Saturday took aim at Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s migration policies for undermining the security of the bloc’s borders. The increasingly isolated Sánchez hit back that his EU partners were responding in a “selfish” and “unlawful” manner to the sudden influx of some 50,000 unauthorized migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa. While almost all those migrants have now returned to Morocco — and none crossed into the EU mainland — the 22 leaders raised “serious concern” over the threat to the EU’s frontier, and zeroed in on Sánchez’s move to grant legal status to up to 1.2 million unauthorized migrants as a “pull factor” that fueled the crisis. Advertisement Advertisement In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote. Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure. “This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June. But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin. “We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on. Advertisement Advertisement In a sign of the increasing threat to the EU’s Schengen open travel area and the explosiveness of migration as a pan-European political issue, the letter’s signatories said they were ready to reinforce or reintroduce “temporary border controls” in the bloc. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gives a press conference on July 28, 2026. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images In addition to Merz and Meloni, the letter was signed by the leaders of Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Sweden. They called for a video conference of interior ministers to agree on next steps. Ireland said it would convene a meeting of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council on Tuesday. Rome and Copenhagen took the initiative in drafting the letter. Sánchez slams ‘selfish’ counterparts In his own letter to von der Leyen, Costa and Martin, Sánchez slammed his European counterparts who “have chosen to attack Spain and to call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen Area.” Italy’s Meloni on Thursday was the first to propose Spain be suspended from the 29-country zone where internal border controls have largely been abolished. Italy on Friday imposed restrictions on free movement from Spain to Italian ports and airports. France has also increased checks on the border with Spain because of the migration surge in Ceuta. Advertisement Advertisement In his letter, seen by POLITICO, Spain’s Socialist prime minister argued that calls to have Spain kicked out of the Schengen zone are “not only contrary to European law, humanitarian law, and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” but also “Europe’s long-term interests and to the most basic common sense.” Sánchez defended himself from accusations that Spain was failing to protect the EU’s external borders, and cited data showing that his country had recorded half as many illegal entries as Italy between 2021 and 2026. He also stressed that it was not the first time that migrants had been weaponized against the bloc’s members, and recalled Belarus’ 2021 bid to sow chaos in the EU by facilitating migrant crossings into Poland and several Baltic countries . Spain’s prime minister added the EU members that had backed the suspension proposal were “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest.” “In the current international context, the European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction,” he wrote. Sánchez’s strongly worded letter underscores the growing tension between the prime minister and the plethora of EU leaders that have expressed support for Spain’s temporary exclusion from the Schengen area. Those calling for action include right-wing politicians such as Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen, a member of the nationalist Finns Party, as well as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, whose Social Democrats belong to the center-left Party of European Socialists. Nicholas Vinocur, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sebastian Starcevic contributed reporting. Advertisement Advertisement

https://georgiatoday.ge/eu-warns-georgia.text: Georgia’s European integration faced renewed uncertainty over the past week as European Union officials criticized the government’s democratic record, the Venice Commission warned that recent legislation undermines political pluralism, and the Constitutional Court prepared to hear a case seeking to ban opposition parties. The developments followed last week’s European Parliament resolution on Georgia and came as the European Commission’s published program for the EU Enlargement Forum, scheduled for November 15–16, listed no representatives of the Georgian government among its confirmed speakers. At the same time, European leaders sought to distinguish their criticism of the authorities from their support for Georgia’s European aspirations, repeatedly emphasizing that the country’s citizens should not lose hope of joining the EU. Georgia absent from EU Enlargement Forum lineup The European Commission’s program for the forum, titled “Wider Europe – Stronger Europe,” includes senior EU officials and leaders from several candidate countries, but no Georgian government representatives. Confirmed speakers include European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos. The program also lists Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic, and North Macedonian Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski. Georgia will be represented in the program by Nino Lomjaria, founder of European Orbit Georgia, who is scheduled to participate in a discussion on civil society and local authorities’ perspectives on enlargement. Euroscope previously reported, citing a source, that the Georgian government had not been invited to the forum. The published program confirms that no government officials are currently listed as speakers, although the absence of names from the program does not, by itself, establish the full circumstances surrounding invitations. The lineup adds to questions about Georgia’s position in the EU enlargement process, particularly as other candidate countries continue to participate in high-level discussions about their European prospects. European leaders tell Georgians not to give up Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal urged the Georgian government to listen to citizens who want their country to join the European Union. “The Georgian government must listen to the people who want to move towards Europe,” Michal told journalists ahead of a European Council meeting. He also called for the EU to open all accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova, arguing that the process should advance for both countries. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola delivered a similar message of support directly to Georgians who continue to campaign for European integration. Asked by Euroscope what she would say to those who remain committed to Georgia’s European future, Metsola replied: “Do not give up. The European Union will always be open to those who look toward it with hope: this is precisely what we tell every country.” She also called for faster progress on accession, emphasizing that each candidate should advance according to its own merits. “We also look forward to accelerated movement on accession, merit by merit per country; that is precisely why we continue our dialogue with all these nations,” she said. The statements show the distinction European officials are making between Georgia’s population and the policies of its government. While support for the country’s European future remains, concerns about democratic standards continue to complicate relations with Tbilisi. EU postpones further discussions until January At the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting on October 13, foreign ministers discussed Georgia but did not reach a new decision. Kallas said the issue would return to the agenda in January. “Democratic backsliding in Georgia is deepening. More opposition parties face the threat of being banned, while the foreign agents law is stifling civil society. The Georgian people want a European future, but Georgian Dream is systematically taking it away from them,” she said. “Our current approach is not creating sufficient pressure for change, nor does it allow us to fully advance Europe’s strategic interests. We will return to this issue in January,” Kallas added. European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos also delivered a direct warning, saying the EU would not cooperate with the Georgian government until it took steps toward European values. Speaking to journalists in Luxembourg ahead of the meeting, she said the bloc wanted to resume active cooperation with the authorities, but that progress depended on government policy. “As long as they are not moving forward and are instead regressing through the laws they have adopted, as long as there is no progress and they do not take steps towards European values, we will not cooperate with them,” Kos said. She stressed that the EU’s position toward the government would not affect its support for Georgian citizens and civil society. “However, we have a very important message for the people of Georgia: although we are not cooperating with the government, we are working with civil society and supporting the people,” she said, adding that assistance would continue in numerous areas. Kos also questioned whether Georgia’s EU candidate status had translated into meaningful progress toward membership. “It would be good if Georgia’s status as a candidate country existed not only on paper, but progress requires the involvement of both sides,” she said. Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže likewise emphasized the difference between the aspirations of the Georgian public and the government’s approach to European integration. “The people of Georgia want to be part of Europe. Unfortunately, the government has not taken the appropriate steps,” Braže told journalists in Luxembourg. Asked about dialogue with the Georgian authorities, she said communication remained possible through diplomatic channels. “We have the embassy in Georgia. Georgians just accredited the new ambassador in Riga, so there is a dialogue,” she said. Braže added that Georgia had not been excluded from international affairs, but that its citizens wanted a different approach to the country’s EU path than the government was pursuing. “Georgia is not excluded from international processes. However, as regards the steps that need to be taken on the path towards the European Union, which is what the Georgian people want, the people want something different from what the government wants,” she said. Ministers also discussed the security implications of EU enlargement and closer cooperation with candidate countries. Kallas emphasized that enlargement represents a strategic investment in Europe’s security, highlighting Ukraine’s role in defending against Russian aggression and the contributions of Moldova and Western Balkan partners to European security initiatives. For Georgia, however, the immediate question remains how to address the concerns that have repeatedly surfaced in discussions with European institutions. Venice Commission criticizes restrictive legislation A newly published opinion from the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on constitutional law, has added to international criticism of Georgia’s legislative direction. The commission examined amendments adopted on March 4, 2026, affecting the Law on Grants, the Organic Law on Political Associations of Citizens, the Criminal Code, and related legislation. It concluded that the amendments impose disproportionate restrictions on fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and association, and undermine political pluralism. The commission also questioned whether the measures achieve their stated objective of protecting Georgia’s sovereignty from foreign interference. “Instead of protecting Georgia’s sovereignty, constitutional order and political parties from foreign influence and external interference, the legislation under review risks fundamentally undermining them,” the opinion stated. The commission warned that broad and imprecise legal definitions could leave civil society organizations, political groups, and individuals uncertain about which activities might trigger government scrutiny or criminal liability. It recommended reconsidering criminal penalties for breaches of grant-related procedures, tightening vague legal definitions, and ensuring that any remaining criminal sanctions are necessary and proportionate. The opinion also called for a more inclusive legislative process and criticized the use of fast-track procedures. The commission expressed regret that Georgian authorities had declined to cooperate in preparing the assessment, while reiterating its willingness to engage in further dialogue. Opposition ban case moves toward hearings Domestic political tensions intensified as the Constitutional Court scheduled hearings for October 21–23 in a case concerning the possible prohibition of opposition parties. Opposition politicians said they had received calls from the court confirming the dates. Irakli Kupradze, a leader of the Lelo–Strong Georgia coalition, described the scheduling as rushed. Berdia Sichinava of For Georgia also confirmed that he had been summoned. The proceedings follow Georgian Dream’s initiative, first announced in October 2025, to seek bans on the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, and Strong Georgia–Lelo. The lawsuit was subsequently expanded to include additional parties, including For Georgia in September 2026. The ruling party has accused the opposition groups of threatening the constitutional order. Opposition figures and European partners, however, have warned that banning political parties would undermine pluralism and democratic competition. Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zurabishvili, criticized the initiative, arguing that it would further isolate the country from Europe and serve Russia’s interests. “This is a direct course of action in line with Russia’s interests,” she said during a Facebook Live broadcast. Zurabishvili also questioned the independence of the Constitutional Court, arguing that it had failed to protect constitutional order and human rights. Her remarks reflect the broader dispute over the independence of state institutions and the future of political competition in Georgia. Giorgi Gakharia, leader of For Georgia, separately accused the authorities of accelerating the proceedings out of fear of losing control over the judiciary. In a statement on X, he described the case as an attempt to eliminate political pluralism. These are opposition allegations, rather than established findings about the court’s motives. For Georgians who continue to support European integration, the message from European leaders has been consistent: the country’s European future remains possible, but concerns about democratic governance and political pluralism cannot be set aside.
